claim_text: Nicaea (325) was about the Arian controversy and the Nicene Creed — NOT the canon.

secondary_sources.citation: Henry Chadwick, The Early Church (Penguin, rev. ed. 1993)
Frances Young, From Nicaea to Chalcedon (Baker Academic, 2nd ed. 2010)

counterargument: Popular skeptic accounts claim Constantine assembled the council to select or suppress scriptures. No primary source supports this; the council's agenda was exclusively Christological and disciplinary.
notes: This is the single most commonly encountered popular misconception in this corpus's subject area. Flagged in Method §2 reference table as explicitly false.

claim_text: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) is the first extrabiblical mention of Israel, as a people not a place.

secondary_sources.citation: James K. Hoffmeier, Israel in Egypt (Oxford University Press, 1997)
Frank J. Yurco, '3,200-Year-Old Picture of Israelites Found in Egypt,' Biblical Archaeology Review 16(5) 1990

notes: The determinative sign on 'Israel' in the stele marks it as a people/ethnic group rather than a territory, which is the basis for the 'people not a place' distinction. This is the scholarly consensus reading.

claim_text: Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem (701 BCE) is the best-corroborated event in the Hebrew Bible.

secondary_sources.citation: William Hallo and K. Lawson Younger, eds., The Context of Scripture, vol. 2 (Brill, 2000)

counterargument: 'Best-corroborated' is a comparative claim. The Assyrian and biblical accounts diverge on outcome — Sennacherib claims tribute and withdrawal; the Bible records an angel destroying the army. The event's occurrence is corroborated; its outcome is contested between sources.
notes: Qualification added: corroboration is for the event, not the outcome. The 'best-corroborated' framing is defensible but should include this distinction in the public text.

claim_text: Paul's undisputed letters (c. 50–60 CE) are the earliest Christian writings that survive and contain no birth narrative, no empty tomb, no biography.

primary_sources.source: 1 Thessalonians, Galatians, 1–2 Corinthians, Romans, Philippians, Philemon
primary_sources.locator: Full texts; see also 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 for the resurrection tradition

secondary_sources.citation: Raymond E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (Doubleday, 1997)

notes: The absence of birth narrative and empty tomb in Paul is a factual observation about Paul's surviving letters, not a theological claim. 1 Cor 15:3–8 does reference resurrection appearances, which should not be conflated with the empty-tomb narratives of the Gospels.

claim_text: Matthew's genealogy is intentionally telescoped and numerically arranged. Omitting generations was compatible with ancient genealogical practice, but the omissions also show that the 3×14 structure is a literary construction rather than an exhaustive pedigree.

secondary_sources.citation: New American Bible, Revised Edition, Matthew 1 notes
Amy-Jill Levine, 'The Jewish Origins of the Christmas Story,' TheTorah.com (2019)
secondary_sources.locator: Sections 'Jesus as a Son of David' and discussion of the fourteen-generation scheme

counterargument: Ancient genealogies could omit generations without functioning as modern exhaustive pedigrees. The qualification is that Matthew's selective structure does not by itself make the genealogy deceptive; it identifies its literary purpose and limits.
notes: NABRE explicitly identifies Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah as omitted and notes the apparent thirteen-name final section.

claim_text: Matthew wants both claims at once — Jesus is Son of David through Joseph's line, and Joseph did not biologically father him.

secondary_sources.citation: Eugene Park, Commentary on Matthew 1:18–25, Working Preacher (2025)
Amy-Jill Levine, 'The Jewish Origins of the Christmas Story,' TheTorah.com (2019)
secondary_sources.locator: Sections 'Jesus as a Son of David' and 'A Miraculous Conception'

counterargument: The legal or adoptive mechanism is an interpretation of Matthew's narrative logic; Matthew does not use modern adoption terminology or provide a biological Davidic line through Mary.
notes: Matthew 1:16 changes the genealogy formula so that Joseph is Mary's husband and Jesus is born from Mary; 1:18–25 excludes Joseph as biological father within the narrative.

claim_text: The two canonical genealogies are textually different. They may have different literary, legal, or theological functions. Later harmonizations exist, but no harmonization can be presented as the explicit explanation of either evangelist.

secondary_sources.locator: Entry identifying Joseph as son of Jacob in Matthew or Heli in Luke

counterargument: Julius Africanus's levirate explanation and the proposal that Luke gives Mary's genealogy are longstanding attempts to reconcile the lists. Neither mechanism is stated in Matthew or Luke.
notes: Matthew runs through Solomon and names Joseph's father Jacob; Luke runs through Nathan and names Joseph as son of Heli.

claim_text: Jeremiah's "write this man childless/without succession" language cannot mean that Jehoiachin literally had no descendants.

secondary_sources.citation: David A. Glatt-Gilad, 'Jehoiachin's Exile and the Division of Judah,' TheTorah.com (2017)

notes: The operative dynastic language in Jeremiah 22:30 concerns a descendant prospering on David's throne and ruling Judah; Chronicles nevertheless lists descendants.

claim_text: Matthew unexpectedly names four women before Mary:

secondary_sources.citation: Amy-Jill Levine, 'The Jewish Origins of the Christmas Story,' TheTorah.com (2019)
secondary_sources.locator: Discussion of the four women in Matthew's genealogy

secondary_sources.citation: Mahri Leonard-Fleckman, 'Judah Meets Tamar “On the Road to Timnah,”' TheTorah.com (2020)
secondary_sources.locator: Genesis 38 discussion of Tamar and Judah

secondary_sources.citation: Elsie R. Stern, 'Kinship over Covenant: The Book of Ruth's Traditional Challenge to Deuteronomy,' TheTorah.com (2025)
secondary_sources.locator: Discussion of Ruth's Moabite identity and Deuteronomy 23

notes: The four are Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the woman Matthew calls 'the wife of Uriah' (Bathsheba). Their intended collective function is interpreted in several ways, so the audit does not impose one exclusive explanation.

claim_text: Mishnah Sotah 4:1, redacted well after the New Testament period, explicitly says a betrothed woman does not drink the bitter water, interpreting Numbers 5's "while under her husband" language as excluding her.

secondary_sources.citation: Sefaria Library, Mishnah Sotah 4:1 with English translation

counterargument: The Mishnah is later than Matthew and cannot simply be projected backward as proof of first-century procedure. It is used only to show that later Jewish interpretation did not treat Numbers 5 as automatically applicable to a betrothed woman.
notes: This is deliberately classified with a qualification because the source is later rabbinic evidence, not direct evidence of first-century courtroom practice.
